Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: Nila was twenty when the assault occurred during a routine hospital visit that quickly became an emergency. She remembers the squeak of the ambulance doors, the sharp intake of breath from the orderly in his navy uniform, and the sudden, jarring movement of a nurse’s gloved hand reaching toward her. In the weeks that followed, the event did not settle into a single story but arrived in disconnected fragments: a flash of the ceiling tiles, the copper taste of blood in her mouth, a half-second of silence before the sirens rose. The memories felt more real than normal, sharp enough that she could taste the antiseptic air and the metallic tang of the night she was cornered. At the same time, she began to believe that if she thought about the event, she would not be able to handle it. Her thoughts became something to be carefully managed, pushed back behind a quiet glass wall. This need for constant vigilance occupied her days. Nila found herself scanning for exits the moment she stepped into any room, her eyes tracking doors, stairwells, and windows as she moved. She had come to expect that unexpected movement nearby could mean danger, so she kept her shoulders slightly hunched, her body ready to shift. Her marriage provided a steady presence, yet she noticed herself pulling back when she saw other couples laughing over morning coffee, their easy closeness feeling like an idealized family picture that did not quite belong to her. The sight of happy families in the street or on television seemed to stand beside her own life without merging with it. Stress accumulated as she adjusted to work at the call center, where the hum of headsets, the blinking of monitors, and the constant flow of clients created a low-grade pressure. She was on guard all the time, certain that the environment was never entirely safe. Over the months, her avoidance took root as quiet habits. When colleagues mentioned the incident or asked how she was holding up, she would nod politely and change the subject, steering clear of reminders that others brought to her attention. The call center itself became a place of subtle tension. Her supervisor wore a crisp blazer and a laminated ID, and Nila found herself stepping back when authority figures approached her cubicle, the uniform triggering the same low alarm she felt in the hospital. She began to release her tension with sexual coping, turning to fantasies and physical release to quiet the constant hum of alertness in her body. At home, this pattern helped her sleep, while her sense of inadequacy rested quietly beside it, a steady certainty that colored how she moved through the world. Now, at twenty-two, Nila sits at her desk during a break, her fingers tracing the edge of her coffee cup while she watches an ambulance pass the glass partition outside. The siren does not make her jump, but her breath catches, and she notes the familiar taste returning to her throat. She has learned to live with the fragments, the scanning, the careful avoidance of reminders and uniformed faces, but the weight of them has grown heavy. What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but the quiet accumulation of days where she felt constantly braced for impact, wondering if she could learn to rest without keeping her eyes fixed on the doors. She hopes to find a space where she can speak about the night without being overwhelmed, where the memories can be held without tasting quite so sharply, and where she can stop measuring herself against an ideal she never quite matched.
